blockers.message: the review record has no `## plan.challenge` section, while roles were active at it

findings.evidence:
export const bucket = (ps: Price[]) =>
  ps.reduce<Record<string, Price[]>>((a, p) => ((a[(p.cents >> 4) & 0x3e8 ? "hi" : "lo"] ||= []).push(p), a), {});
findings.recommendation: A developer who has not seen the plan cannot answer "what makes a price premium?" from this line: the rule is hidden in `(p.cents >> 4) & 0x3e8`, a shift and a bitmask with no name and no comment, while the docstring talks of "cheap" and "premium" and the keys say "lo" and "hi". The reader is likely to assume a threshold comparison, but a bitwise AND of selected bits is not one (e.g. 16000 cents gives 1000 & 1000 → "hi", 16384 cents gives 1024 & 1000 → 0 → "lo"), so the shape hides what the code actually does. On top of that the line combines a `reduce` with a comma-operator return, `||=` lazy init inside an index expression, single-letter names (`ps`, `a`, `p`) and an untyped `Record<string, …>` result whose keys only appear as string literals. Rewrite it as a named function with a named threshold constant in cents and an explicit comparison (`const PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS = …; const isPremium = (p: Price) => p.cents >= PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS;`), a plain loop or two `filter` calls, and a typed result such as `{ cheap: Price[]; premium: Price[] }` whose keys match the docstring; if the bitmask really is the intended rule, a comment must say why.
findings.title: `bucket` packs its rule into an unreadable one-liner with a magic bitmask
